praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-001.prompt: A district newsletter describes a middle-school garden: families tend beds after dismissal, science classes measure soil moisture, and ELA students keep field notes. The principal writes that the project is “not an add-on but the place where observation becomes writing.” Which statement best captures the principal’s main idea?

options.a: The garden is meant to turn firsthand looking into academic writing
options.b: Families volunteer mainly so the district can skip hiring a science aide
options.c: Soil measurement is the only skill the garden is designed to teach
options.d: After-school tending is meant to replace the school’s ELA curriculum

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-001.explanation: The quoted line ties observation in the garden to writing. Supporting details (families, soil, notes) illustrate that claim; they are not competing theses. The piece does not argue for cutting staff, teaching only science, or dropping ELA.

distractorExplanations.b: Invents a staffing motive the newsletter never states; family tending is a detail, not the claim.
distractorExplanations.c: Elevates one supporting activity (soil work) into the whole purpose; the principal stresses writing.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the garden as a replacement for ELA rather than a site where ELA work happens.

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-002.prompt: After a wetlands article, Ms. Ortiz sees that students can copy sidebar definitions but cannot explain why the marsh was drained. She drops the glossary quiz for a prompt: “Using two details from the article, explain what was lost.” The next week several students ask for the article again before writing. What inference is best supported?

options.a: Students already knew the marsh history from a field trip last year
options.b: Earlier tasks could be finished without actually using the article
options.c: The glossary quiz covered more content than the new writing prompt
options.d: Ms. Ortiz intends to drop informational reading from the rest of the unit

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-002.explanation: Students could parrot definitions yet failed a task that required article details, then requested the article once the task demanded it. That pattern supports the inference that prior work did not require the text. Field trips, quiz breadth, and dropping reading are not in the passage.

distractorExplanations.a: Adds an unmentioned field trip; the evidence is about quiz work versus article-based writing.
distractorExplanations.c: Compares coverage the passage never measures; the issue is whether the article had to be used.
distractorExplanations.d: Overreads a task change as abandoning informational reading, which she still requires.

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-003.prompt: An op-ed says branch libraries should keep late July hours because “the students who lose the most pages also lose the most hours of air-conditioned quiet.” After noting bus-route cuts, the writer urges the city council to restore evening hours rather than fund a one-day book giveaway. The author’s primary purpose is to

options.a: Explain how air-conditioning units in branch libraries actually work
options.b: Praise the one-day book giveaway as the strongest summer reading plan
options.c: Persuade the council to keep evening library hours during July
options.d: Claim that bus-route cuts have no relationship to student reading time

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-003.explanation: The piece is an op-ed with a policy ask: restore evening hours instead of a one-day giveaway. Air-conditioning and bus cuts are reasons, not the purpose. The giveaway is the plan the author rejects, and bus cuts are presented as relevant, not irrelevant.

distractorExplanations.a: Mistakes a supporting image (cool quiet space) for a how-to on HVAC systems.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the recommendation; the giveaway is the alternative the author wants dropped.
distractorExplanations.d: Contradicts the writer, who cites bus cuts as part of why evening hours matter.

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-004.prompt: A researcher reporting on a phonics pilot writes, “Early gains were real, but they were tempered by uneven attendance in two classrooms.” As used in this sentence, tempered most nearly means

options.a: Canceled completely by the attendance problems
options.b: Treated as the study’s single strongest finding
options.c: Invented so the pilot would appear more successful
options.d: Reduced in strength by another competing factor

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-004.explanation: “Gains were real, but…” signals that attendance did not erase the gains; it limited how strongly they can be claimed. That is the “moderated/reduced” sense of tempered. Canceled, celebrated, and invented ignore the contrast the “but” sets up.

distractorExplanations.a: Goes too far: “real, but tempered” means limited, not wiped out entirely.
distractorExplanations.b: Fits a word like “highlighted,” not a hedge that weakens how far the gains go.
distractorExplanations.c: Reads “tempered” as fabrication; the sentence still calls the gains real.

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-005.prompt: A superintendent argues that every elementary school should buy a $12,000 listening lab because “one third-grade teacher said her class loved the headphones last April.” Which evaluation of that argument is most accurate?

options.a: It treats one classroom anecdote as if it proved a district-wide need
options.b: It is strong because April is a typical month for audio-lab purchases
options.c: It is strong because the dollar figure is stated to the nearest thousand
options.d: It fails only because headphones cannot be used for listening practice

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-005.explanation: The conclusion is district-wide spending; the support is one teacher’s liking in one month. That is a classic overgeneralization from an anecdote. Calendar typicality, a precise price, and denying that headphones can be used for listening do not repair the leap.

distractorExplanations.b: Month typicality does not turn one liking report into evidence for every school.
distractorExplanations.c: A precise cost is not evidence of need; it only specifies the proposed expense.
distractorExplanations.d: Headphones can support listening; the flaw is the evidence leap, not the device.

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-006.prompt: A professional article contrasts round-robin oral reading with partner retell. In the first, one student reads while others wait; in the second, both partners must reconstruct the gist. The author concludes that wait-time, not print itself, is what drains comprehension in round-robin. What is the author’s central claim?

options.a: Round-robin works because listeners hear a more fluent oral model
options.b: Round-robin loses comprehension mainly because classmates sit idle
options.c: Partner retell works only after students have already memorized the text
options.d: Print difficulty, not idle wait-time, is what the author blames for weak recall

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-006.explanation: The concluding sentence names wait-time—not print—as the drain on comprehension. That is the claim partner retell is meant to fix. Praising fluent models, requiring memorization, and blaming print all contradict the author’s stated contrast.

distractorExplanations.a: Credits round-robin with a benefit the author does not claim; idle waiting is the problem named.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds a memorization condition the article never sets for partner retell.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the conclusion: the author rejects print difficulty as the main cause.

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-007.prompt: A study summary reports that after 20 minutes of outdoor recess, third graders’ on-task time in the next lesson rose, while indoor free-play in the gym produced a smaller rise. Both groups had the same snack. Which inference is best supported?

options.a: Snack quality, not the recess setting, caused the on-task difference
options.b: Indoor gym play pushed on-task time below the no-recess baseline
options.c: Outdoor recess was tied to a larger on-task gain than gym free-play
options.d: Third graders cannot stay on task unless recess lasts a full hour

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-007.explanation: The summary compares two conditions with the same snack: outdoor recess produced a larger on-task rise than gym play. It does not report a no-recess baseline, a one-hour requirement, or snack as the cause—snack was held constant.

distractorExplanations.a: Snack was the same in both groups, so it cannot explain the difference.
distractorExplanations.b: Gym play still produced a rise; nothing says it fell below a no-recess baseline.
distractorExplanations.d: The study used 20 minutes; it does not say an hour is required for any on-task time.

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-008.prompt: A historian introduces a 1918 teacher’s diary by noting that the entries “were never meant for publication; they record ration lists and who was absent, not speeches.” She then asks readers to notice how often influenza, not the planned curriculum, decides the day’s work. Her purpose in this introduction is mainly to

options.a: Argue that 1918 teachers published their lesson plans as books
options.b: Prove that influenza had no effect on school attendance that year
options.c: Entertain readers with a wholly invented classroom from the 1910s
options.d: Frame the diary as a private record of disruption rather than oratory

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-008.explanation: The introduction tells readers how to read the source: private, mundane, and shaped by influenza, not public speechmaking. That is framing purpose. Publication, “no effect,” and fiction all contradict the historian’s cues.

distractorExplanations.a: Contradicts “never meant for publication”; the diary is not presented as a published plan book.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the hint to notice how often influenza decides the day.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a diary introduction as fiction; the historian presents a historical source.

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-009.prompt: A committee “was willing to endorse longer independent-reading blocks, but only if it could qualify that endorsement: gains appeared when books matched reading level, not when time alone increased.” In this sentence, qualify most nearly means

options.a: Limit the endorsement by attaching a condition
options.b: Celebrate the endorsement in a public speech
options.c: Withdraw the endorsement without any explanation
options.d: Translate the endorsement into another language

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-009.explanation: The “but only if” clause shows qualify in the academic sense: restrict a claim. The condition is matched books, not time alone. Celebrate, withdraw, and translate ignore that limiting move.

distractorExplanations.b: Fits “publicize,” not a hedge that narrows when the endorsement applies.
distractorExplanations.c: The committee still endorses; it does not take the statement back.
distractorExplanations.d: Language change is irrelevant; the issue is the scope of the claim.

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-010.prompt: A PTA flyer says scores rose the year interactive whiteboards were installed, so the boards caused the rise. Which challenge most weakens that causal claim?

options.a: Whiteboards cost more than ordinary paper wall charts
options.b: The same year the district also hired extra reading specialists
options.c: Students often enjoy looking at colorful classroom screens
options.d: Some rooms still have unused chalk trays under the new boards

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-010.explanation: The flyer infers cause from one year’s coincidence. Another change in that same year—new reading specialists—is an alternate cause that breaks the leap. Price, enjoyment, and leftover chalk trays do not explain the score change.

distractorExplanations.a: Cost does not address whether the boards produced the score increase.
distractorExplanations.c: Enjoyment is not evidence against (or for) a causal effect on scores.
distractorExplanations.d: Leftover hardware is irrelevant to what caused the year’s score change.

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-011.prompt: A columnist notes that hallway “grit” posters name persistence but never name sleep, meals, or bus reliability. She writes that “character slogans become a way to blame children for adult systems.” Which statement best states her main idea?

options.a: Hallway posters are the most effective way to teach persistence
options.b: Children fail mainly because they refuse to eat the school meals
options.c: Character slogans can hide adult failures behind student blame
options.d: Bus reliability has no connection to whether students persist

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-011.explanation: The quoted sentence is the thesis: slogans shift blame from adult systems onto children. Meals and buses are examples of those systems, not a claim that children refuse food or that buses are unrelated. She is criticizing posters, not endorsing them as the best teaching tool.

distractorExplanations.a: Praises the posters; the columnist is criticizing what they leave out.
distractorExplanations.b: Turns meals into student refusal; she uses meals as an adult-system example.
distractorExplanations.d: Denies a link she implies by listing buses among unnamed adult conditions.

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-012.prompt: An essay’s body follows one colonial apprentice from dawn to supper; a footnote lists typical weekly wages for three trades. What does that arrangement most strongly suggest about the author’s emphasis?

options.a: The wage figures are invented and should be ignored by readers
options.b: The footnote is meant to replace the narrative as the essay’s thesis
options.c: The author thinks wages matter more than the boy’s daily routine
options.d: The day’s story is the focus; wages sit as supporting background

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-012.explanation: Body text carries the narrative emphasis; a footnote typically credits or tucks a narrow data aside. Wage lists support without becoming the thesis. Nothing says the figures are fake, and putting wages in a note argues they are secondary, not primary.

distractorExplanations.a: A footnote can still be evidence; placement is not a signal that data are fake.
distractorExplanations.b: Footnotes do not replace the thesis; the body still carries the main story.
distractorExplanations.c: If wages were the priority, they would more likely occupy the body, not a note.

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-013.prompt: Writer A: “Weekend packets keep skills from fading between Friday and Monday.” Writer B: “Weekend packets mainly sort students by who has a quiet table and a parent free to sit nearby.” The two writers disagree primarily about whether weekend homework

options.a: Functions chiefly as practice or as a screen for home resources
options.b: Should be printed in color instead of ordinary black and white
options.c: Is assigned more often in high school than in the third grade
options.d: Must be scored by a computer rather than by a classroom teacher

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-013.explanation: A claims a learning function (practice against fade); B claims a sorting function (home quiet and adult time). Print color, grade band, and scoring method are not the clash in the two statements.

distractorExplanations.b: Neither writer discusses ink color; the split is purpose, not printing.
distractorExplanations.c: Grade level is not compared; both speak to weekend packets in general.
distractorExplanations.d: Scoring method is unmentioned; they disagree about what the packets measure.

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-014.prompt: “The attendance chart does not introduce a new claim; it is there to underscore the author’s point that absences cluster on assembly days.” As used here, underscore most nearly means

options.a: Contradict and then replace the author’s stated point
options.b: Emphasize or reinforce the point already being made
options.c: Hide the author’s point from anyone reading quickly
options.d: Postpone the author’s point until a later chapter

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-014.explanation: The chart “does not introduce a new claim”; it supports the existing one about assembly-day absences. That is reinforce/emphasize. Contradict, hide, and postpone fight the “does not introduce a new claim” cue.

distractorExplanations.a: A chart that backs an existing claim is not contradicting or replacing it.
distractorExplanations.c: Support graphics are meant to make the point clearer, not to conceal it.
distractorExplanations.d: The sentence places the chart with the current point, not a later chapter.

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-015.prompt: An author claims a new basal reader “fails because it never mentions local rivers,” citing only that her own class lives near a river. The weakest part of this argument is that it

options.a: Names a river the class could actually visit on a later field trip
options.b: Admits that some students enjoy stories set in other regions
options.c: Treats one class’s local setting as the standard for all readers
options.d: Notes that basal readers are sold in more than one U.S. state

praxis-core-readiness-check-reading-015.explanation: The conclusion is that the basal fails as a reader; the evidence is one classroom’s nearby river. That overextends a local preference into a general standard. Field-trip possibility, enjoyment of other settings, and multi-state sales are not the logical gap.

distractorExplanations.a: A possible field trip does not create the overgeneralization; the sample size does.
distractorExplanations.b: The prompt does not include that admission; it is not the stated weak step.
distractorExplanations.d: Multi-state sales might even strengthen a demand for broader settings; it is not the cited flaw.
